name: OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker
what_it_holds: The official 'Track the Recovery' repo (Chetty/Friedman/Hendren/Stepner/team, Harvard/Opportunity Insights). data/ folder has committed CSVs at National/State/County/City x Daily/Monthly granularity for Affinity Solutions credit/debit card spending ('Affinity - National - Daily.csv', 'Affinity - State - Daily.csv', 'Affinity - County - Daily.csv', 'Affinity - City - Daily.csv', plus Monthly variants, and 'Affinity Income Shares' / 'Affinity Industry Composition' breakout files by income quartile and industry, back to Jan 2020 with a 2019 pre-period baseline index). Repo also bundles other Track-the-Recovery series (Womply small-business revenue/open, Burning Glass job postings, Zillow rent) in the same data/ tree per its data dictionary, 1,892+ commits, actively updated. Docs include a Data Dictionary (md + PDF), Data Documentation (source/processing notes), and a Data Revisions log (evidence of point-in-time-ish revision tracking, worth checking for vintage use). Data is a public good; must credit provider + cite the paper (https://opportunityinsights.org / tracktherecovery.org), no resale/redistribution to third parties as raw data.
why_useful: Directly targets gap #6 (public consumer-spend panels; the gap list explicitly names 'OpenTable seated diners' alongside this exact project) and doubles as a leisure/restaurant/entertainment demand proxy (Affinity card-spend 'Arts & Entertainment' and 'Restaurants & Hotels' categories, Womply restaurant revenue, Google Mobility 'retail & recreation') that could nowcast US regional consumer leisure strength feeding into ABNB nights/ADR by region. Caveat: series thin out after 2023, so utility is mostly historical/backtest, not current nowcasting — flag for the team to check the live tracktherecovery.org site vs. this repo's freshness before relying on it for 2026 quarters.
time_coverage: 2020-01 to ~2023-06 for most series (repo itself last pushed 2026-09-12; unclear if data files still update)

license: none declared (custom attribution terms in README)

name: OECD-Weekly-Tracker
what_it_holds: Official OECD Weekly Tracker of GDP growth repo (author is the OECD economist behind the tracker). Data/ folder holds committed Excel and CSV files: weekly_tracker.csv (1.57MB), weekly_tracker_level.csv (6.47MB), weekly_tracker_yoy.csv, plus matching .xlsx versions, monthly_tracker*.xlsx (5 variants), quarterly_tracker*.xlsx (4 variants), and a Weekly_Tracker_Excel.xlsx human-readable book. Covers ~46 OECD/G20 countries, weekly frequency built from a Google-Trends panel via ML model (consumption, labour, housing, trade, industrial activity, sentiment signals), back to pre-2020 with continuous updates (repo pushed as recently as 28 Aug 2026). No explicit license file found.
why_useful: Directly the named theme item (OECD Weekly Tracker). A weekly, cross-country GDP-growth nowcast built from Google Trends could proxy travel-adjacent consumer demand/labor conditions in ABNB's key geographies (EMEA, LatAm, APAC) at higher frequency than Eurostat tour_ce_omr (addresses gap #4 mixed-frequency/nowcasting methods and partially gap #6 consumer spend panels); git history of the CSVs could be mined for a point-in-time vintage series, which is explicitly on the missing-gaps list (#4).

name: cfpb/consumer-credit-trends-data
what_it_holds: Official CFPB repo backing the 'Consumer Credit Trends' site. Committed CSV files (plus JSON used by cfpb-chart-builder) split into four market folders: auto-loans, credit-cards, mortgages, student-loans. Each market has origination counts and dollar volumes, YoY % changes, state-level annual changes, and demographic cuts (borrower age, credit score tier, neighborhood income). Many series indexed to Jan-2009 baseline; monthly cadence; updated as recently as 2 Sep 2026 per repo activity. No stars/license metadata surfaced but repo is under the official cfpb GitHub org (public-domain CC0 pattern used by other cfpb repos).
why_useful: Direct, free, monthly, point-in-time-able proxy for US consumer credit health (credit-card originations/credit tightness) — feeds the 'consumer strength' driver in the ABNB nights/ADR model and is a genuine Fed/CFPB-adjacent consumer credit series (gap area: consumer credit/BNPL theme; adjacent to gap #6 consumer spend panels). Credit-card credit tightness and delinquisyncratic segments could be tested as a leading indicator for discretionary travel spend.
time_coverage: index base Jan 2009 to present, monthly
size_hint: multiple CSV/JSON files across 4 market folders, unknown total row count
